## Beyond the lottery: what else changed? {#d2s1-p01 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{webr}
#| context: setup
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
#| include: false
library(estimatr)
gw <- read.csv('evaluation_data_GreenWaste_simple.csv')
city <- subset(gw, setting == 'city')
# Stack the two periods: each business has two rows (after = 0 before GreenWaste, after = 1 twelve months after).
long <- data.frame(business = rep(city$business, 2),
  after = rep(0:1, each = nrow(city)),
  took_part = rep(city$took_part, 2),
  cost = c(city$cost_before, city$cost_after))
# Warm up estimatr while the opening slides are discussed: its first call in the browser is slow.
invisible(lm_robust(cost ~ after, data = long[1:200, ], clusters = business))
```

We return to the **city**, with 4,794 participant businesses and 5,206 comparison businesses that did not receive GreenWaste. Participation followed the score rule, **not a lottery**.

<div class="comparison-pair"><div><h3>Before and after: −669 AED</h3><p>What else changed over the year?</p></div><div><h3>With and without: −1,638 AED</h3><p>How different were the groups already?</p></div></div>

::: {.ask}
Could comparing **the changes in both groups** help?
:::

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Two minutes independent recall, two minutes compare reasons, one minute city orientation. Programme is equipment subsidies, installation help and training. Same annual waste cost outcome, measured before and 12 months after. Say: "Today we use another method, with a different group of businesses that were not chosen at random, and ask what else changed." Do not treat the pilot as the city's true effect. Open webR early for one optional arithmetic demo. Transition: inspect what actually changed in both city groups.
:::

## How much more did participants' costs fall? {#d2s1-p02 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d4_lines())
```

::: {.ask}
Which change should we subtract from which?
:::

**H4-A, the difference-in-differences study summary, on worksheet page 1** describes this comparison. Solid lines join the observed means. Each business was measured only twice.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Read population, axes, period and both directions before arithmetic. Participant businesses 1,432 to 763; comparison businesses 2,258 to 2,401. Programme-start marker indicates between the two measurements, not an additional observed wave or precise start date. Different starting levels do not alone invalidate DiD. Ask predictions, not answers from a formula yet. Transition: work the two changes, then the difference.
:::

## Use four numbers to find the difference in differences. {#d2s1-p03 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

Use **Q1 on worksheet page 3**. Work alone, then compare.

1. Participant businesses: **763 − 1,432 ≈ −669 AED**.
2. Comparison businesses: **2,401 − 2,258 ≈ ______ AED**.
3. The difference between the two changes: **participant change − comparison change**. This is the **difference-in-differences (DiD) estimate**.

<button data-open="d4-arithmetic" data-closed="Check the difference between the two changes" data-opened="Hide the calculation" aria-controls="d4-arithmetic" aria-expanded="false">Check the difference between the two changes</button>
<p id="d4-arithmetic" class="calculation-output" hidden>−669 − (+143) ≈ <strong>−812 AED</strong>.</p>

::: {.ask}
Is this the same as the difference between the two groups after the programme?
:::

::: {.notes}
8 minutes. Preserve Fiona's four-number task. Two minutes work, three minutes pair/group check, three minutes collect signs/units and reveal. Use unrounded means for final -812.446; one-AED display discrepancies acceptable. Q1 includes a blank plot to annotate, not another method exercise. A negative difference between the two changes means a larger reduction in costs for participant businesses. Not automatically an established effect. Transition: run the regression that gives the same difference from individual records.
:::

## We run the regression in R. {#d2s1-p04b .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

We create the **interaction variable** and run the regression. The trainer runs the box and the table appears below it.

```{webr}
#| echo: true
# long has two rows per business: after = 0 before GreenWaste, after = 1 twelve months after.
# The interaction is 1 only for participant businesses in the after period.
long$after_x_took_part <- long$after * long$took_part
# clusters = business allows for each business being measured twice.
fit <- lm_robust(cost ~ after + took_part + after_x_took_part,
  data = long, clusters = business, se_type = "stata")
summary(fit)
```

::: {.ask}
Which row of the table is the difference between the two changes, and which line of code creates it?
:::

You do not need to write or run R. Q2 on your worksheet asks you to read the table.

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. Prediction first, then one Run by the trainer. Walk through the comments, not the syntax; participants do not code. The stacked table `long` and the estimatr package are prepared in the hidden setup cell, so the box is only the interaction and the regression. The after_x_took_part row is the DiD estimate, -812 AED, interval -833 to -792. Estimates 2,258 (Intercept), 143 (after), -826 (took_part), -812 (after_x_took_part). The same four numbers appear in the printed table on the next slide. clusters = business is the reason the interval allows for the repeated measurement. If the runtime is slow or unavailable, go straight to the printed table on the next slide within the same time.
:::

## Which row shows the difference between changes? {#d2s1-p05 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(sub('^<p[^>]*>.*?</p>', '<p class="caption">City annual cost (AED), before and after. Reference: comparison businesses before GreenWaste.</p>', sub('<p class="caption">.*$', '', d4_regression())))
```

<div class="review-annotate"><button data-table-column="1" aria-pressed="false">Coefficient</button><button data-table-column="2" aria-pressed="false">Interval</button><button data-table-column="3" aria-pressed="false">P-value</button></div>

::: {.ask}
**Q2:** Find *after × took part*: the difference between the two changes. What do the other rows show?
:::

::: {.notes}
5 minutes. H4-A table, page 1. Reference is comparison businesses before, 2,258. After row is the comparison businesses' +143 change. Participant row is initial gap -826. Interaction -812 is the difference between the two changes, not the participants' own -669 change or their after mean. Highlight columns, then annotate row on paper. Intercept meanings depend on reference coding. Model cost ~ after*took_part, business-clustered robust interval -833 to -792. Avoid coefficients as causal magic. Transition: draw the missing no-programme participant outcome.
:::

## The dashed line is an assumption {#d2s1-p06 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<div id="d4-path"><div data-variant>',d4_lines(),'</div><div data-variant hidden>',d4_lines(TRUE),'</div></div>'))
```

<button data-swap="d4-path" data-closed="Show the assumed untreated path" data-opened="Show observed means only" aria-pressed="false">Show the assumed untreated path</button>

Under the **parallel trends assumption**, the participant businesses' cost without GreenWaste would also have risen by **143 AED**, to about **1,575 AED**. The numbers on the graph are the rows of the regression table on the previous slide.

::: {.ask}
Is the dashed participant outcome observed, or is it assumed?
:::

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Predict before reveal. After the reveal, point out that the graph carries the regression rows: 2,258 is the Intercept (comparison businesses before), +143 is the after row, -826 is the took_part row (the gap before) and -812 is the after:took_part row (observed 763 minus the assumed 1,575). Dashed path hypothetical counterfactual, not additional measured data. 1,432 +143 approximates1,575; assumed path to observed763 yields812 gap. Parallel trends concerns untreated changes, not equal cost levels. Source §3/page1 and visual/page2. Have learners add dashed path to Q1 blank plot and state assumption in Q3. Transition: what could make untreated changes differ?
:::

## Could the groups differ without GreenWaste? {#d2s1-p07 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<div class="review-grid"><div><h3>A shared change</h3>',d4_scenario(1),'<p>Both groups\' costs move together, for example when a service charge rises for every business.</p></div><div><h3>A different change</h3>',d4_scenario(2),'<p>A service charge only for the kinds of business that did not take part, for example different pricing or a tax on equipment they already have.</p></div></div>'))
```

These are **hypothetical costs without GreenWaste**. They are not facts about the GreenWaste data.

::: {.ask}
**Q3 (e) on page 4:** What evidence would help check the second possibility?
:::

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. Two minutes think/request, three minutes pair explanation, two minutes feedback. Read the pictures before the question: same axes, same programme start, no GreenWaste in either. Left: both groups spike at the same point after the start and then level out at a higher cost, so the comparison businesses' change is a fair stand-in and the difference between the two changes would be close to zero. Right: only the comparison businesses spike, for example from different pricing or a tax on equipment they already have, and then level out higher while participant businesses stay flat. A difference-in-differences calculation would show participants' costs falling relative to the comparison even though GreenWaste did nothing. The lines look alike before the start in both pictures, which is why earlier history helps but does not settle the question. Need comparable absolute untreated changes for this additive cost DiD, not automatically equal percentage rises. Accept charge schedules linked to business types, concurrent policies, changing business mix or measurement. Note composition/measurement and anticipation/spillovers alongside parallel trends when relevant; no new checklist lecture. A city's shared time period alone is insufficient. Transition: earlier histories could help assess plausibility.
:::

## Which earlier history would make you hesitate? {#d2s1-p08 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<div class="review-grid"><div><h3>A</h3>',d4_trend(1),'</div><div><h3>B</h3>',d4_trend(2),'</div></div>'))
```

These two earlier cost histories, A and B, are **hypothetical** and use the same scales. They are not additional GreenWaste observations.

<button data-open="d4-trend-answer" data-closed="Check your reason" data-opened="Hide feedback" aria-controls="d4-trend-answer" aria-expanded="false">Check your reason</button>
<p id="d4-trend-answer" class="feedback" hidden>In history B, the two groups were already changing differently. History A is more reassuring, but it cannot prove what would have happened after the programme.</p>

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Q3: choose individually and explain feature to partner before feedback. A shows equal changes at different levels; B participant costs already falling while comparison businesses rising. Same cost and time axes. Do not infer real group histories from these examples. No significance test proves parallel trends; several earlier measures help credibility, not certainty. Transition: do we have those earlier measures in this file?
:::

## Can one earlier measurement show a trend? {#d2s1-p09 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d4_timeline())
```

::: {.ask}
Could the GreenWaste data show whether earlier cost trends were similar?
:::

We would ask for **several earlier measurements in both groups**, and for an explanation of any other changes. Even reassuring earlier histories cannot prove what would have happened after the programme.

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Q3 evidence request, then distinguish supplied/absent information in H4-A §4. One baseline is a level, not a trend. Do not invent a test or substitute pilot control-group changes as proof about this city's different population. The file has the same records/two waves; stable composition doesn't establish parallel trends. Transition: separate causal credibility from the size needed for the decision.
:::

## Precise estimate. Does it meet the 1,000 AED rule? {#d2s1-p10 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d4_interval())
```

::: {.ask}
**Q4:** How do the estimate and the interval compare with our rule of a reduction of at least **1,000 AED**?
:::

The interval describes statistical uncertainty **if the model's assumptions hold**. It does not settle whether parallel trends holds, and it does not allow for every source of bias.

::: {.notes}
6 minutes. Estimate812, reductioninterval792-833, both below rule. Reverse negative interval endpoints when converting scale. p<.001/intervalexcludingzero are not proof of causal validity or practical sufficiency. Say conditional on model, not certainty of the true effect if assumptions fail. The fictional rule is annual saving per participant. Transition: read the source as a report reader, not just a calculator.
:::

## What does the study summary support? {#d2s1-p11 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

Read **H4-A, the difference-in-differences study summary, on worksheet page 1**. Work alone first.

Circle the last row of the table, which gives the difference between the two changes, with its units and its interval.

Underline the **assumption**. Mark the **limit of the data** that prevents a check of earlier trends.

::: {.ask}
On **page 4**, write one interpretation that H4-A supports and one specific evidence request.
:::

::: {.notes}
9 minutes. Five independent reading/annotation, two pair source-check, two feedback. Source identifies physical paragraphs/table rather than a separate unknown report. Do not reteach all questions; use completed Q1-Q4. Listen for the difference between the two changes, conditional on credible untreated trends, not an established effect from arithmetic alone. Require request and decision purpose. Transition: AI can report correct numbers but fabricate assurance.
:::

## Does the comparison support the AI's causal claim? {#d2s1-p12 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<p class="caption">Authored exercise response, not a real AI answer. Read the full prompt and response on worksheet page 5.</p><div class="ai-reading">',d4_paragraphs(d4_ai),'</div>'))
```

::: {.ask}
**Page 5:** Mark supported claims and overclaims. Check H4-A, the study summary on **page 1**.
:::

::: {.notes}
8 minutes. Five markup, three source-based debrief. Restore old realistic table-explanation device with corrected812, interval792-833 and richer qualification. Written for the exercise, with no answer highlighting and no run of the naive prompt. Supported group changes/estimate/precision and benefit of comparing changes. Unsupported: same follow-up period proves parallel trends, interval proves robustness/attribution, clears1000rule/national guarantee. Different levels accounted for is legitimate mechanics, not proof of untreated trend. Monitoring caveat does not repair unsupported claims. Transition: constrain next prompt to source and missing evidence.
:::

## Ask the AI for an explanation you can check. {#d2s1-p13 .reader-slide .s1-review .d2s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(paste0('<p class="caption"><strong>Improved prompt, worksheet page 5.</strong> Copy it and H4-A, the study summary, into Microsoft Copilot.</p><div class="better-prompt">',d4_paragraphs(d4_prompt),'</div>'))
```

::: {.ask}
Which claim improved? What still needs checking against H4-A?
:::

The final box on **page 4** is extra: write one interpretation H4-A supports and one evidence request on your own if you like.

Next, we use a different comparison: businesses on either side of the score cut-off.

::: {.notes}
7 minutes. Four run, three compare; Snapshot total15. No account setup. Page6 prepared response is same-task paper alternative if delayed/unavailable. Ask questions first; source/correctness, not AI agreement, is check. No mandatory second chat or extra best-practice slide. Compare interaction interpretation, causal assumptions, uncheckable pre-trend claim and threshold. Transition: the final box on page 4 is optional extra work; move on to the score cut-off comparison (Session 2). The removed closing slide and the removed repeat-the-calculation slide free about 12 minutes; use them as buffer.
:::
